interest: Shows wartime salmon research, Japanese fishing-fleet security fears in Mexico and Brazil, and postwar Yale occupation training.
overview: This file from State Department decimal file 894.628 (Animal Husbandry, Japan: Fisheries) covers records from August 1940 through December 1944 relating to Japanese fisheries, fishing vessels, and related wartime security and postwar planning. It includes interdepartmental correspondence and an extensive 1942 scientific report from the Department of the Interior's Fish and Wildlife Service on salmon resources and migrations in Bristol Bay and the Bering Sea, an investigation initially launched to assess Japanese fishing encroachment in Alaskan waters before being curtailed by World War II. The file also documents diplomatic, naval, and consular surveillance of Japanese fishing vessels, floating crab canneries, and trawlers across the Western Hemisphere, including sightings off Alaska, legal actions in Honolulu, Mexican seizures and internment of Japanese vessels and crews off Lower California following Pearl Harbor, and stringent security restrictions and citizenship revocations imposed on Japanese fishermen in Santos, Brazil. In addition, the file contains correspondence from Yale University's Civil Affairs Training School inviting State Department fisheries experts to lecture officers preparing for the military occupation and civil administration of postwar Japan.

subfiles.about: Scientific investigations of the red salmon populations, oceanography, offshore migration routes, and inshore river escapements in Bristol Bay and the Bering Sea.
subfiles.from: Fish and Wildlife Service, Department of the Interior
subfiles.summary: This excerpt from the Fiscal Year 1942 Alaska Fishery Investigations Report reviews biological research on the red salmon resources of Bristol Bay. It covers oceanographic surveys conducted with the Coast Guard vessel Redwing, offshore experimental gillnetting along the Aleutian chain using the chartered vessel American Star, and inshore surveys of adult spawning escapement and fingerling migration across five major river systems. The offshore findings revealed that red salmon inhabit the continental shelf broadly and migrate through passes west of Unimak, contradicting earlier migration assumptions. Operations were suspended for the duration of the war due to military call-ups of personnel and the vicinity of active combat zones.
subfiles.title: Excerpt from Alaska Fishery Investigations Report for Fiscal Year 1942 on Bristol Bay Salmon Resources
